title: Storyworth, Remento and Memorygram: Life-Story Books for Parents and Grandparents
subtitle: How these story-book services work, what your parent actually has to do, and what to check before you buy one as a gift.
excerpt: Storyworth, Remento and Memorygram turn a parent's answers to weekly questions into a printed keepsake book. Here is how each one works and what to ask about cost before you order.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Most families have a few stories that get told at every holiday dinner, and many more that never come up at all. How did Grandpa end up in that town? What was Mom's first job really like? Once those memories are gone, nobody can ask anymore.

A small group of companies now offer a gentle way to collect those stories. Over several weeks or months, your parent answers one question at a time, and the answers become a hardcover book. AARP has an article about asking parents for their stories while you still can. It is for AARP members, and its tags name Storyworth and Remento. The details below come from the companies' own pages, and we did not find an independent review of any of the three.

These are not gadgets you plug in. They are services that end with a printed book. You, the gift giver, set up an account. Then questions go out to your parent on a schedule, usually once a week. Your parent answers, and the company gathers the answers into book pages, often with family photos added.
The big differences are in how your parent answers and in what the finished book can do.

items: Storyworth sends one question a week by email or text. Your parent can reply to the email, type on the website, or tell the story over the phone, where it is transcribed word for word (turned into written text). Storyworth says it works on any phone, even a landline. Upgraded plans add Magic Interviews, which turn a phone conversation into a written story, and Family Calls, where a relative joins in.

Remento is built around speaking rather than writing. Your parent simply talks, and their voice plays back on every page of the book. In the company's words, it "Works on any phone, no app or login needed."

Memorygram lets your parent type, use voice-to-text (speaking while the phone writes it down), or take scheduled phone interviews. A QR code, a small square pattern you scan with a smartphone camera, is printed in the book and plays their voice.

sections.content: One honest limit applies to all three: the book is only as good as the answers. A parent who finds weekly questions a chore may quietly stop, and the book will be thin.

items: Know the full cost. Storyworth is a yearly plan, so ask what happens at renewal, what extra copies cost and what shipping costs. Memorygram says there are "No recurring subscription fees," but check at checkout whether extra contributors or permanent audio storage cost more. Remento's price was not listed on its main page; confirm it at checkout.

Match the answering style to your parent. A letter writer may enjoy typing. Someone who would rather speak than write may prefer Remento, which says no writing is required, or Storyworth's phone option.
Check whether voice is included. If hearing a parent's voice matters to you, confirm which plan includes audio and how long recordings are kept.
Watch the calendar. Printing and shipping take time, especially before Christmas. If you are late, look for digital delivery or a gift certificate instead.
Read the privacy policy. Voice recordings and family photos are personal. See how each company stores them and for how long.
Ask about help with questions. Storyworth lets family edit questions or write their own. Memorygram lets you choose up to 60 questions.

sections.content: Setting it up so your parent finishes

The easiest way to help is to do the setup yourself. Create the account, enter your parent's phone number or email, and pick the first few questions together. Start with easy, cheerful ones, such as a favorite childhood meal, before moving to bigger topics.

If your parent likes company, join a phone session or sit beside them while they answer. Memorygram says others can be invited to contribute, and photos can be added, which may take some pressure off one storyteller.

Keep the pace relaxed. Memorygram's page says answering three questions a week gets its book ready by Christmas 2026, but that is the company's own claim and depends on when you start, so check the dates before you count on it. There is no prize for speed. A finished book in spring is better than an abandoned one in December.

These books are not a good fit for everyone. Someone who dislikes talking about the past may find weekly questions tiresome, and a parent living with memory loss could find them upsetting. If you are unsure, ask your parent first, or talk with their doctor or care team about what feels comfortable.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A life-story book takes a little patience from everyone. Pick the service that fits the way your parent likes to talk, check the full price and the delivery dates, and then let the stories come at their own pace.

products.name: Storyworth Memoirs
products.blurb: Suits a parent who likes to write or chat, since stories can come by email reply, the website or a phone call that works even on a landline. It is a yearly plan, so confirm renewal and extra-book costs.

products.name: Remento Life Story Book
products.blurb: A good match for someone who would rather talk than type: no writing is required, it works on any phone with no app or login, and their voice plays back on every page of the hardcover book.

products.name: Memorygram
products.blurb: For families who prefer to avoid a subscription: the company says there are no recurring subscription fees. Answers can be typed, spoken or given in phone interviews, and a printed QR code plays the storyteller's voice.
